sections.content: A classical numerical course covering many concepts of computational mathematics, but not deep in each aspect.
sections.teaching: Good and clear teaching. Prof. Peng has a good understanding and organization of the materials.
sections.grading: Grading mainly based on assignments and final project. Very nice and kind grading. Not hard to get A.
sections.workload: Not heavy. The usual assignment will involving coding part, while Prof. Peng will offer examples which you just need to modify a little bit to solve the problems. The final project is just as same as common assignment. But Prof. Peng may switch from such final project to an exam.

sections.content: Introduces common numerical methods, including FDM, FVM and FEM, as well as commonly used iterative solvers.
sections.teaching: The teacher is very knowledgeable and uses handwritten notes in class, but some of the fonts may look messy and need to be carefully checked and confirmed.
sections.grading: If you submit your homework on time and meet the requirements, the teacher will give you full marks.
sections.workload: There are four assignments, a final project, and a take-home exam. Since there is a lot of knowledge involved, you may need to spend time digesting it. But I believe that after carefully reviewing and organizing what you have learned, you will gain a lot.

sections.content: This course covers many numerical schemes in details. Most of those methods are related to solving pde problems. It would be useful for students working on research problems in related areas.
sections.teaching:
1. No typed notes. No typed notes. No typed notes. Only handwritten notes are provided (with artistic handwriting).
2. Presentation is not that easy to follow.
sections.grading: HW gives full mark once you make the submission. Though full mark is given, the instructor will look into all submissions and provide detailed feedback.
sections.workload:
4-5 hws, 1 project, 1 take-home exam.
No attendance is required.

sections.content: Suitable for students researching numerical solutions of partial differential equations.The content is also relatively fundamental, mainly involving finite difference methods.
sections.teaching: the teacher will personally derive equations and can promptly upload the derivation process from the classroom to Canvas on the same day of teaching.Towards the end of a class, a thought-provoking question will be posed, and the answer to the question will be discussed in the next session.
sections.grading: The final grade is based on assignments (50%) + the final project (50%)The final exam will be a take-home project.
sections.workload: There will be 6-8 homework assignments (including computer projects).

sections.content:
The material is not that easy to read, for an engineering student. There are several applications that are very theoretical and I would say not very appropriate for my purpose. However, I do think that for someone from a math background, it is okay and is very detailed.

I think the course covered the main differential equations. I just think that there should be more lessons on how to apply it well, especially in certain kinds of engineering equations and scenarios.
sections.teaching: The professor is good in teaching and is very enthusiastic. What I like about him is he seems to be really enjoying what he teaches. He shows up on time in class and is always available for consultation. He explains concepts well but for very complex ones, he has a hard time explaining it to students from non-math backgrounds.
sections.grading: The grading is okay and quite lenient, but still is fair. For instance, a well-done homework normally receives around 9/10 or 10/10. The grading also takes too long, probably at the end of the term. So you don't have a good gauge on how your grades are.
sections.workload: For me, I think there are too many homework, considering this is a PG course. Although I have expected it based on stories by other students. There are many homework that are given weekly or every other week. Each homework typically has 3-4 questions, but they have sub-questions, which make them longer. There is also a final project wherein you have to choose any differential equation from your field and present your numerical assessment about it. It's quite flexible, which is pretty nice.

sections.content:
The course covers different numerical methods applied to PDEs. There were 6 parts to the course:
1. Finite difference method
2. Stability and Truncation error analysis
3. Variational principle and finite element method
4. Convergence analysis and error estimates
5. Spectral method
6. Finite Volume Method
sections.teaching: Prof. Wang was quite a good teacher and was able to explain the concepts quite clearly. The lecture notes are a bit messy and hard to understand by themselves, so I recommend going to class (or watching the lecture videos).
sections.grading:
4 Homeworks (40%)
Take home final project (60%)

Me:
Homeworks: 95.8/100
Final Project: 100/100
Overall: 98.3/100
Grade: A

Very easy to get a good grade, but to get an A+ you have to be careful (I only made 2 minor mistakes in the homeworks)
sections.workload:
The workload of the course is very light. (although we only had 4 homeworks instead of the planned 8-10 for some reason). The homeworks are just applying proofs/concepts we learned in the lecture to other problems.

We had two weeks to do the take-home project, which was also similar to the HWs but required us to do some simulation (using MATLAB or another programming language). There were only 3 problems so it only took a day or two to do.

sections.content: Not going to repeat what the previous review mentioned. He decomposed the content of "Numerical Solution of Partial Differential Equations: An Introduction" by K. W. Morton (up to Ch. 7?) into several parts. He also added the relaxation methods (originally from 5312?)
sections.teaching: Better attend his lectures because he would add (e.g. more examples or more detailed steps) on the lecture notes during the lessons. The textbook would be a good supplement to the lecture notes in case you want some more examples. However it is painful if you only read the textbook, and you may miss something else he taught.
sections.grading:
Assignments 40%
Final project 60%

Xiaoping do us good grading the project. I thought I didn't explain the idea in one part clear enough but he still gave me full mark.

Edit: but it turns out, as Aaron mentioned, that the A/A+ cutoff is very strict, so...
sections.workload:
Has coding for both assignments and finals but the codes can be pretty easily googled. Any language would be good but Xiaoping prefers Matlab(/Octave).

Other than that the written portion of the project is quite challenging because it takes time to think about what the questions want to know.
